blocks.p: But there were three of those who had come from the land of Doubting who, after roaming the country a while and seeing that they had escaped, were bold enough to push their way into Mansoul, knowing there were still Diabolonians in the town. (Three, did I say? I think there were four.) And to whose house should these Diabolonian doubters go, but to the house of an old Diabolonian in Mansoul named Evil-Questioning, a very great enemy to Mansoul and a great doer among the Diabolonians there. To his house, then, they came (you may be sure they had directions for finding it), and he made them welcome, pitied their misfortune, and gave them the best he had. After a little acquaintance (and it was not long before they had that), old Evil-Questioning asked the doubters whether they all came from one town; he knew they all came from one kingdom.
“No,” they answered, “nor even from one county.”
“I,” said one, “am an Election-doubter.”
“I,” said another, “am a Calling-doubter.”
Then the third said, “I am a Salvation-doubter,” and the fourth said he was a Grace-doubter.

“Well,” said the old gentleman, “be from whatever county you like, I can see you are down on your luck, lads. But you are exactly my measure, you are one with my heart, and you shall be welcome here.”
So they thanked him, and were glad to have found themselves a harbor in Mansoul.
Then Evil-Questioning said to them, “How many of your company came with you to the siege of Mansoul?”

“There were only ten thousand doubters in all,” they answered, “for the rest of the army was made up of fifteen thousand Bloodmen. These Bloodmen border on our country; but, poor men, we hear that every one of them was taken by Emmanuel’s forces.”
“Ten thousand!” said the old gentleman. “I promise you, that is a good round company. But how did it happen that so mighty a number lost heart and did not dare to fight?”
“Our general,” they said, “was the first man to run for it.”
“And who, if you please,” said their landlord, “was that cowardly general of yours?”

“He was once the Lord Mayor of Mansoul,” they said. “But please don’t call him cowardly; you would be hard put to name anyone, from the east to the west, who has done more service for our prince Diabolus than my Lord Incredulity. Still, if they had caught him, they would certainly have hanged him; and we promise you, hanging is a bad business.”
Then the old gentleman said, “I wish all ten thousand doubters were in Mansoul now, well armed, and I at the head of them. I’d see what I could do.”
“Yes,” they said, “that would be a fine thing to see. But wishes, alas! What are they?” And these words were spoken aloud.
“Well,” said old Evil-Questioning, “don’t talk so loudly. You must lie low and keep quiet while you are here, or I assure you, you’ll be snapped up.”
“Why?” said the doubters.

“Why!” said the old gentleman. “Why! Because the Prince and the Lord Secretary, and their captains and soldiers, are all in town at present; yes, the town is as full of them as it can hold. And besides, there is one named Willbewill, a most cruel enemy of ours, whom the Prince has made keeper of the gates and commanded to search out and destroy, with all the diligence he can, every Diabolonian of every kind. And if he lights on you, down you go, even if your heads were made of gold.”

And now see how it happened. One of the Lord Willbewill’s faithful soldiers, Mr. Diligence by name, had been standing all this while under old Evil-Questioning’s eaves, and heard all the talk between him and the doubters under his roof.
This soldier was a man my lord trusted greatly and loved dearly, both because he was a man of courage and because he never tired of hunting down Diabolonians to arrest them.
Now this man, as I told you, heard it all; so what does he do but go to his lord and tell him what he had heard.
“Do you say so, my trusty man?” said my lord.
“Yes,” said Diligence, “I do; and if your lordship will be pleased to come with me, you will find it just as I have said.”
“And are they there?” said my lord. “I know Evil-Questioning well, for he and I were close in the days of our falling away from the King; but I don’t know where he lives now.”
“But I do,” said his man, “and if your lordship will go, I will lead you to his den.”
“Go!” said my lord. “That I will. Come, my Diligence, let us go and find them out.”
So my lord and his man went straight to the house, his man going ahead to show him the way, until they came right under old Mr. Evil-Questioning’s wall.
“Listen, my lord,” said Diligence. “Do you know the old gentleman’s voice when you hear it?”
“Yes,” said my lord, “I know it well, though I haven’t seen him for many a day. This much I know: he is cunning. I hope he doesn’t give us the slip.”
“Leave that to me,” said his servant Diligence.
“But how shall we find the door?” said my lord.
“Leave that to me too,” said his man.

So he led my Lord Willbewill around and showed him the door. Then my lord, without more ado, broke it open, rushed into the house, and caught all five of them together, just as Diligence had told him. So my lord arrested them, led them away, and handed them over to Mr. Trueman the jailer, who on his orders locked them up. In the morning my Lord Mayor was told what my Lord Willbewill had done during the night, and his lordship rejoiced greatly at the news, not only because doubters had been arrested, but because old Evil-Questioning was taken; for he had been a very great trouble to Mansoul and a great affliction to my Lord Mayor himself. He had often been sought, but no one had ever laid a hand on him until now.

The next thing was to prepare for the trial of these five prisoners in Mr. Trueman’s keeping. So the day was set, the court was called and assembled, and the prisoners were brought to the bar. My Lord Willbewill had power to slay them on the spot when he took them; but he thought it more for the honor of the Prince, the comfort of Mansoul, and the discouragement of the enemy to bring them out for public judgment.

But, as I say, Mr. Trueman brought them in chains to the bar in the town hall, for that was the place of judgment. So, to be brief, the jury was empaneled, the witnesses were sworn, and the prisoners were tried for their lives. The jury was the same one that had tried Mr. No-Truth, Pitiless, Haughty, and the rest of their companions.

And first, old Questioning himself was set at the bar, for he was the one who had received, entertained, and comforted these doubters, who by nation were foreigners. He was told to listen to his charge, and that he was free to object if he had anything to say for himself. So his indictment was read, in this form:

“Mr. Questioning, you are indicted here by the name of Evil-Questioning, an intruder upon the town of Mansoul, because you are a Diabolonian by nature, a hater of the Prince Emmanuel, and one who has studied the ruin of Mansoul. You are also indicted for countenancing the King’s enemies, though wholesome laws forbid it. For, first, you have questioned the truth of her doctrine and her standing; second, you have wished that ten thousand doubters were in her; and third, you have received, entertained, and encouraged her enemies, who came to you from their army. What do you say to this indictment? Are you guilty or not guilty?”

“My lord,” he said, “I don’t know what this indictment means, since I am not the man it concerns. The man accused here is called Evil-Questioning, and I deny that the name is mine. Mine is Honest-Inquiry. The one does sound like the other, I grant; but your lordships know, I think, that there is a wide difference between them. For I hope that a man, even in the worst of times, and among the worst of men, may make an honest inquiry into things without running the risk of death.”

Then my Lord Willbewill spoke, for he was one of the witnesses. “My lord, and you, the honorable bench and magistrates of the town of Mansoul, you have all heard the prisoner at the bar deny his name, thinking to slip out from under the charge. But I know him to be the man it concerns, and that his proper name is Evil-Questioning. I have known him, my lord, for more than thirty years; for he and I (it is a shame for me to say it) were close acquaintances when Diabolus, that tyrant, governed Mansoul. And I testify that he is a Diabolonian by nature, an enemy to our Prince, and a hater of the blessed town of Mansoul. In the times of rebellion, my lord, he has stayed at my house no fewer than twenty nights together, and we used to talk then much as he and his doubters have talked lately. It’s true I haven’t seen him for many a day. I suppose the coming of Emmanuel to Mansoul has made him change his lodgings, just as this indictment has driven him to change his name. But this is the man, my lord.”
Then the court said to him, “Have you anything more to say?”

“Yes,” said the old gentleman, “I have. For all that has been said against me so far comes from the mouth of one witness; and it is not lawful for the famous town of Mansoul to put any man to death at the mouth of one witness.” [Deut. 17:6]

Then Mr. Diligence stood up and said, “My lord, as I was on my watch one night at the head of Bad Street in this town, I happened to hear a muttering inside this gentleman’s house. ‘What’s going on here?’ I thought. So I crept up very quietly to the side of the house to listen, thinking, as indeed it turned out, that I might come upon some secret meeting of Diabolonians. As I drew nearer and nearer, right up to the wall, I soon realized there were foreigners in the house; but I understood their speech well, for I have been a traveler myself. Now, hearing such talk in such a tumbledown cottage as this old gentleman lived in, I put my ear to a hole in the window and heard them talk as follows. This old Mr. Questioning asked these doubters who they were, where they came from, and what their business was in these parts; they answered every question, and still he entertained them. He also asked how many of them there were, and they told him ten thousand men. Then he asked them why they had made no more manly assault on Mansoul, and they told him; and he called their general a coward for marching off when he should have fought for his prince. Further, this old Evil-Questioning wished, and I heard him wish it, that all ten thousand doubters were in Mansoul now, and himself at their head. He also told them to lie low; for if they were taken they must die, even if they had heads of gold.”

Then the court said, “Mr. Evil-Questioning, here now is another witness against you, and his testimony is full. First, he swears that you received these men into your house and fed them there, though you knew they were Diabolonians and the King’s enemies. Second, he swears that you wished ten thousand of them were in Mansoul. Third, he swears that you advised them to lie low and keep quiet, so that they would not be taken by the King’s servants. All of this shows that you are a Diabolonian; for if you had been a friend to the King, you would have arrested them.”

Then Evil-Questioning said, “To the first of these I answer: the men who came into my house were strangers, and I took them in. Has it now become a crime in Mansoul for a man to entertain strangers? That I fed them as well is true; and why should my charity be blamed? As for the reason why I wished ten thousand of them in Mansoul, I never told it to the witnesses, nor to the men themselves. I might have wished them here so that they would be taken, and so my wish may have meant well to Mansoul, for all anyone yet knows. I did also tell them to take care not to fall into the captains’ hands; but that might be because I am unwilling that any man should be slain, and not because I wanted the King’s enemies, as such, to escape.”

My Lord Mayor then replied that though it was a virtue to entertain strangers, it was treason to entertain the King’s enemies. “And as for whatever else you have said,” he went on, “you are only laboring with words to evade judgment and put off its execution. But even if nothing more could be proved against you than that you are a Diabolonian, for that alone you must die by the law. But to be a receiver, a feeder, an abettor, and a harborer of others of them, yes, of foreign Diabolonians, yes, of those who came from far away on purpose to cut off and destroy our Mansoul: this must not be borne.”
“I see how the game will go,” said Evil-Questioning. “I must die for my name, and for my charity.” And so he held his peace.

Then they called the foreign doubters to the bar, and the first of them to be arraigned was the Election-doubter, the one who doubted God’s choosing of his own. His indictment was read; and because he was a foreigner, the substance of it was told him through an interpreter: namely, that he was charged with being an enemy of Emmanuel the Prince, a hater of the town of Mansoul, and an opponent of her most wholesome doctrine.

Then the judge asked him whether he would plead. But all he would say was that he confessed he was an Election-doubter, and that this was the religion he had always been brought up in. “And moreover,” he said, “if I must die for my religion, I think I shall die a martyr, and so I care the less.”

To this the judge replied: “To question election is to overthrow a great doctrine of the gospel: namely, God’s knowledge of all things, his power, and his will. It is to take away God’s freedom to do as he pleases with his own creature, to trip up the faith of the town of Mansoul, and to make salvation depend on works, and not on grace. It also gives the lie to the Word, and unsettles the minds of the men of Mansoul. Therefore, by the best of laws, this man must die.”
Then the Calling-doubter was called and set at the bar. His indictment was in substance the same as the other’s, except that he was particularly charged with denying the calling of Mansoul.
The judge asked him, too, what he had to say for himself.

He replied that he had never believed there was any such thing as a distinct and powerful call of God to Mansoul, other than the general voice of the Word; and not even that, except in so far as it urged men to refrain from evil and to do what is good, with a promise of happiness attached to doing so.

Then the judge said, “You are a Diabolonian, and you have denied a great part of one of the truths of the Prince of Mansoul most proved by experience. For he has called, and she has heard a most distinct and powerful call from her Emmanuel, by which she has been brought to life, awakened, and filled with heavenly grace, so that she desires fellowship with her Prince, to serve him, to do his will, and to look for her happiness purely from his good pleasure. And for your hatred of this good doctrine, you must die.”
Then the Grace-doubter was called, and his indictment was read, and he answered it.

“Though I am of the land of Doubting,” he said, “my father was the offspring of a Pharisee, and lived respectably among his neighbors; and he taught me to believe, and believe it I do and will, that Mansoul shall never be saved freely by grace.”

Then the judge said, “Why, the law of the Prince is plain. First, negatively: ‘not of works.’ Second, positively: ‘by grace you are saved.’ [Eph. 2:8-9] And your religion rests in and on the works of the flesh; for the works of the law are the works of the flesh. Besides, by saying what you have said, you have robbed God of his glory and given it to a sinful man. You have robbed Christ of the necessity of what he undertook, and of its sufficiency, and given both of these to the works of the flesh. You have despised the work of the Holy Spirit, and have magnified the will of the flesh, and of the legal mind that hopes to be saved by keeping the law. You are a Diabolonian, the son of a Diabolonian; and for your Diabolonian principles you must die.”

Having gone this far with them, the court sent out the jury, who promptly brought them in guilty of death. Then the Recorder stood up and addressed the prisoners: “You, the prisoners at the bar, have been indicted here and proved guilty of high crimes against Emmanuel our Prince, and against the welfare of the famous town of Mansoul, crimes for which you must be put to death; and so you shall die.” So they were sentenced to the death of the cross. The place appointed for their execution was the place where Diabolus had drawn up his last army against Mansoul; except that old Evil-Questioning was hanged at the top of Bad Street, directly across from his own door.
